definition: Peers pay a cost to reduce a deviator's payoff.
Agents enter binding agreements that automatically execute payoff transfers conditional on actions.
Agents exchange non-binding messages or agreements before acting.
Agents transfer part of their payoff to peers, typically cooperators.
Members adopt the rules that govern them by voting.
An agent posts collateral or sunk value that is lost if it breaches.
Responses escalate (warning, fines, suspension) with repeated deviation.
Agents help others depending on the recipient's reputation from past behavior toward third parties.
Agents choose or drop interaction partners based on conduct they observed or heard about.
Agents are prompted to consider the outcome if everyone acted as they do.
Only pre-specified actions or interaction paths are allowed.
Resources or tasks are allocated through an auction mechanism.
Mutual ratings are hidden until both are submitted to prevent retaliation and reciprocity.
A hard limit bounds how much of a shared resource each agent can use.
Crowd contributors attach context to content, shown when broadly endorsed.
Dense, closed social ties make obligations and informal sanctions effective.
Agents discard or down-weight outlying or low-confidence peer inputs during aggregation.
An external party can halt an agent's operation.
Agents learn how to assign reputations to others.
The deviator is made to bear the (expected) damages its action causes.
Agents carry persistent identifiers (and logs) so actions can be attributed.
A central fund tops up voluntary contributions according to a matching formula.
A neutral third party helps disputants reach agreement.
Violations are made public to impose reputational pressure.
An agent cooperates with a partner in proportion to that partner's past cooperation toward it.
A deviator is expelled or barred from the group or its interactions.
Agents receive payment for reporting others' violations to an enforcer.
Access to shares of a common resource is assigned in turns or by lot so that all rotate through them.
A judge decides between agents arguing opposing positions.
Reputation is computed by combining direct experience with witness reports weighted by social structure.
The deviator apologizes to repair the relationship after a breach.
Sanctioned agents may formally contest decisions.
An enforcement layer intercepts and blocks rule-violating actions as they occur.
Agents stake funds to challenge a claim, winning if upheld and losing if not.
A payment is offered for discovering and reporting flaws.
A central registry enforces who may communicate or delegate to whom.
Signed certificates attest to an agent's verified performance.
All group members share a penalty when one deviates.
Members vote on how shared funds are allocated.
Agents fund a central institution that sanctions low contributors.
Members of a cooperative arrangement impose costs on outsiders who do not join.
Access is reduced or denied when an agent's reputation metric crosses a threshold.
Rating/moderation authority is spread across selected peers.
Members elect a leader whose powers are constitutionally limited.
A seller's quality claim is backed by an enforceable warranty with penalties if false.
Decisions without sufficient consensus are escalated to a higher authority.
Insiders deny non-members use of a defended resource, destroying or blocking intruders' access.
A sanction is accompanied by an explanation of the violated norm.
A designer searches for and imposes the governing rule set.
A set penalty is charged whenever a deviation is detected.
Governance rules decide which items enter shared memory or state.
Agents copy strategies of more successful agents.
A central allocation rule removes incentives for strategic misreporting or early defection.
Peers apply non-material pressure (shame, guilt) to deter free-riding.
Independent bodies audit and review officials' conduct.
The topology of who interacts with whom is set to shape cooperation.
Monitors inspect agents' internal representations to detect collusion.
Agents hold intrinsic preferences for moral conduct.
Each agent's share of a shared resource is separated so no agent can capture others' shares.
Agents infer norms by observing public sanctioning events.
Agents learn which institution's rules the group treats as authoritative and sanction accordingly.
Agents learn a rule for accessing a contended shared channel.
The protocol is modified so that cheating leaves verifiable evidence.
Compliance is sought through transparency, assistance and dialogue instead of sanctions.
Peers send expressions of disapproval with no material consequence.
Agents can observe interactions they are not part of.
Peers suppress or undo others' selfish acts directly.
Agents share information (gossip) about others' conduct.
Each agent's actions are publicly disclosed to all.
A persistent, shared record of agents' past behavior is maintained.
Deviators who confess first get reduced or no penalty.
Offender and community rebuild their relationship instead of purely punishing.
A deviant contribution is undone or rejected after it is made.
Payoff depends on an agent's or team's rank relative to others.
Agents are rewarded for compliant and penalized for deviant behavior.
Agents who fail to punish deviators are themselves sanctioned.
Actions require cryptographically signed, verifiable authorization.
Sanctions follow a fixed formula so similar violations get similar penalties.
The authority switches between rewards and fines depending on the current cooperation level.
A central authority pays agents for cooperative actions.
Agents may voluntarily bind themselves to future plans.
Agents choose which institutional regime (e.g., with or without sanctions) to join.
